content.text:
**I’d start with Teal’s free plan** if you’re applying to multiple jobs. It combines a resume builder with application tracking and lets you create unlimited resume versions, though free AI writing is limited. That makes it my default pick without knowing your budget or career stage. ([tealhq.com](https://www.tealhq.com/pricing?utm_source=openai))

I’d narrow the choice to these:

| Tool | When I’d choose it | Cost and main limitation |
|---|---|---|
| **Teal** | You want to tailor resumes **and organize your job search**. | Free tier; Teal+ is **$29 every 30 days**. Free AI credits and keyword matching are limited. ([tealhq.com](https://www.tealhq.com/pricing?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Rezi** | Your priority is **AI-assisted resume writing**, with keyword targeting and resume feedback. | Free tier includes **one resume and three PDF downloads**; Pro is **$29/month**. ([rezi.ai](https://www.rezi.ai/pricing?utm_source=openai)) |

**My recommendation:** Try Teal free first. If you mainly need help drafting and rewriting bullet points rather than managing applications, try Rezi’s free tier instead. I wouldn’t buy a subscription until you’ve tested it with your actual resume and one target job.

Whichever you choose, require the AI to preserve your facts—no invented skills, responsibilities, or performance numbers—and review every bullet before submitting.

**What kind of job are you targeting, and do you already have a resume or need to build one from scratch?**

annotations.title: Jobscan Tutorial | What Is Jobscan and How Do You Use It?
Jobscan Tutorial | What Is Jobscan and How Do You Use It?
Jobscan vs. Resume Worded: Which Gets You a Job Faster in 2026?

content.text:
**Jobscan is worth trying for free; paying is worthwhile mainly if you’re tailoring lots of applications.** I’d treat it as a résumé-checking tool—not a way to guarantee interviews.

### Where it helps
Jobscan compares your résumé with a specific job description and flags missing skills, keywords, and potential ATS issues. Its strongest use is catching relevant experience you already have but haven’t described clearly in the employer’s language. ([jobscan.co](https://www.jobscan.co/jobscan-tutorial?utm_source=openai))

I’d consider paying if you:
- Are actively applying to many similar roles.
- Want a repeatable check before submitting each application.
- Find that its free reports uncover useful omissions—not just wording changes.

### Where I’d be skeptical
**Its match score is not the employer’s hiring verdict.** It measures résumé-to-posting alignment; even Jobscan’s documentation says measurable results don’t factor into the match rate. So I wouldn’t sacrifice clear achievement bullets or add skills you don’t have just to raise the number. ([jobscan.co](https://www.jobscan.co/jobscan-tutorial?utm_source=openai))

I’d skip paid access if you only need a couple of checks, already tailor effectively, or mainly need help explaining your achievements rather than identifying keywords.

### Cost and subscription catch
Current pricing is about **$49.95/month or $89.95 every three months**. The quarterly offer includes a seven-day trial. Subscriptions renew automatically, and cancellation does not automatically produce a refund. ([jobscan.co](https://www.jobscan.co/blog/jobscan-vs-resume-worded/?utm_source=openai))

**My recommendation:** Try the free version on two or three jobs you genuinely qualify for. Pay for a short period only if the feedback meaningfully improves your résumé or saves enough time. Don’t keep paying merely to chase a higher score.

What kinds of roles are you applying for—and are you getting interviews already?

### Which I’d choose

- **Already have a résumé you like, but want targeted feedback? Jobscan.** Its upload-and-compare workflow is a good fit for that specific task. ([jobscan.co](https://www.jobscan.co/blog/jobscan-vs-teal/?utm_source=openai))

annotations.title: How to Read an Applicant Resume: Resume Review Tips
How to Read an Applicant Resume: Resume Review Tips
How to Read an Applicant Resume: Resume Review Tips
How to Read an Applicant Resume: Resume Review Tips
Talent Matching - Data Processing FAQ – Greenhouse Support

content.text:
**Recruiters generally scan for a match first, then read for evidence.** It’s less “Let me learn your whole story” and more “Does this person look relevant enough to interview?” The exact process varies, but initial scanning followed by closer evaluation is a common approach. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&hl=en&utm_source=openai))

### 1. First pass: “Is this plausibly a fit?”
They look for basic alignment:
- Relevant experience and skills.
- Required qualifications.
- Employment history that fits the role.

At this stage, the question is whether you meet the requirements—not whether every bullet is impressive. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&utm_source=openai))

**My advice:** Make your target role and strongest relevant experience easy to spot. Don’t make someone piece together your fit from scattered clues.

### 2. Closer read: “What have they actually done?”
If the initial fit is there, they examine your experience, skills, and qualifications more carefully before deciding whether to move you to a screening call or interview. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&utm_source=openai))

**My advice:** Write bullets that give evidence rather than just name responsibilities. For example, a hypothetical rewrite:

> **Vague:** “Responsible for customer onboarding.”  
> **Specific:** “Redesigned onboarding for 40 enterprise accounts, reducing average setup time from 12 days to 8.”

Use real numbers when available; otherwise describe scope, complexity, or a concrete outcome.

### 3. Decision: “Is there enough here to justify a conversation?”
Resume review is a screening step, not the final hiring decision. The immediate outcome may simply be an invitation to a phone screen. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&utm_source=openai))

**My advice:** Optimize for a clear, credible case—not a complete autobiography. Put the most relevant evidence first, explain unfamiliar job titles, and cut material that doesn’t help establish fit.

### What about the ATS?
Software may come before or alongside human review. Some systems extract titles, skills, dates, and experience; some employers enable AI-assisted matching. There isn’t one universal screening process across employers. ([support.greenhouse.io](https://support.greenhouse.io/hc/en-us/articles/41131616864283-Talent-Matching-Data-Processing-FAQ?utm_source=openai))

**A useful test:** Give someone your resume for a brief glance, then ask: “What role am I suited for, and what’s the strongest evidence?” If they can’t answer, make those two things more obvious.

annotations.title: What Your Resume Is Up Against
Ladders Updates Popular Recruiter Eye-Tracking Study With New Key Insights on How Job Seekers Can Improve Their Resumes
What Your Resume Is Up Against

content.text:
**Sometimes for an initial skim—but “six seconds per résumé” isn’t a universal rule.**

The claim comes from a **2012 study by the job site TheLadders**, which tracked the eye movements of **30 recruiters**. It reported roughly six seconds to make an initial “fit/no fit” decision—not necessarily the total time spent evaluating a candidate. ([forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/susanadams/2012/03/26/what-your-resume-is-up-against/?utm_source=openai))

A **2018 update reported 7.4 seconds**, again specifically for the initial screening. That’s evidence of a quick first pass, not a deadline that every recruiter follows. ([prnewswire.com](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/ladders-updates-popular-recruiter-eye-tracking-study-with-new-key-insights-on-how-job-seekers-can-improve-their-resumes-300744217.html?utm_source=openai))

There are reasons to be cautious: the original sample was small, and the research came from a commercial career-services company. It doesn’t establish how every recruiter reviews every résumé across industries and hiring situations. ([forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/susanadams/2012/03/26/what-your-resume-is-up-against/?utm_source=openai))

**My practical takeaway: make your fit easy to spot, rather than trying to make your entire résumé readable in six seconds.** I’d prioritize:
- Clear job titles, employers, and dates.
- Relevant qualifications near the top.
- Short accomplishment bullets rather than dense paragraphs.
- Enough detail to reward a closer read.

Think **“easy to skim, useful to read,”** not “six seconds or you’re out.”

content.text:
**One page is a good default—not a hard rule.** For most U.S. job applications, one or two pages is acceptable. ([case.edu](https://case.edu/studentlife/careercenter/career-development/career-resources/tips-job-seekers/resumes/resume-format?utm_source=openai))

- **If you’re a student or recent graduate:** aim for one page. ([bc.edu](https://www.bc.edu/bc-web/offices/studentaffairs/sites/careers/prepare/resume.html?utm_source=openai))
- **If you have substantial relevant experience:** two pages are fine; don’t cut strong accomplishments just to meet a one-page target. ([careerservices.fas.harvard.edu](https://careerservices.fas.harvard.edu/resources/gsas-masters-resume-cover-letter/?utm_source=openai))
- **Keep it readable:** don’t squeeze everything into tiny text or eliminate white space. Prioritize relevant content and clean formatting. ([cloudfront.careeronestop.org](https://cloudfront.careeronestop.org/Veterans/JobSearch/ResumesAndApplications/resume-overview.aspx?utm_source=openai))

My practical test: **Does page two add compelling evidence that you’re qualified, or just more history?** If it’s mostly older, unrelated jobs or repetitive duties, I’d trim it.

How many years of experience do you have, and what kind of role are you applying for?

content.text:
**Not necessarily—one typo isn’t an automatic rejection.** It depends on the mistake, the hiring manager, and the role; an editing job may put more weight on it than other positions. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/career-advice/resumes-cover-letters/typo-on-resume?utm_source=openai))

If you’ve already submitted it:
- **Minor spelling or punctuation error:** I’d fix your master copy rather than send an apology just to flag it. Small errors don’t always warrant resubmitting. ([enhancv.com](https://enhancv.com/blog/typo-on-resume/?utm_source=openai))
- **Wrong contact information or a typo that changes your qualifications:** Send a corrected version with a brief note so they have accurate information. ([resumespice.com](https://resumespice.com/i-submitted-my-resume-with-a-mistake-what-do-i-do/?utm_source=openai))
- **Portal lets you replace the document:** Upload the corrected copy there. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/career-advice/finding-a-job/reapply-for-a-job?utm_source=openai))

Don’t count yourself out over this. **What was the typo, and what role are you applying for?**

annotations.title: AI for Resumes and Cover Letters – Harvard FAS | Mignone Center for Career Success
AI for Resumes and Cover Letters – Harvard FAS | Mignone Center for Career Success
Unsuccessful resume parse – Greenhouse Support
Using AI In Your Job Search – Office of Career Strategy – Yale University

content.text:
**An AI resume checker can be useful, but treat it as an editing assistant—not a hiring verdict.** Career services at Harvard recommend using AI to improve application materials while also getting human feedback. ([careerservices.fas.harvard.edu](https://careerservices.fas.harvard.edu/ai-resumes-and-cover-letters/?utm_source=openai))

Its usefulness depends on what you’re checking:

- **Writing and relevance:** It can help refine wording and identify skills from a job description that your resume should address—provided you actually have those skills. ([careerservices.fas.harvard.edu](https://careerservices.fas.harvard.edu/ai-resumes-and-cover-letters/?utm_source=openai))
- **Formatting:** Warnings about complex layouts can be legitimate. Greenhouse, an applicant tracking system (ATS), documents parsing problems with some formatting, including contact information placed in headers, footers, or text boxes. However, that doesn’t establish that any particular checker accurately simulates an employer’s system. ([support.greenhouse.io](https://support.greenhouse.io/hc/en-us/articles/200989175-Unsuccessful-resume-parse?utm_source=openai))
- **Accuracy of your experience:** You still need to verify every suggestion and keep the resume faithful to your background. Yale recommends starting with your own work rather than relying on AI-generated material. ([ocs.yale.edu](https://ocs.yale.edu/channels/using-ai-job-search/?utm_source=openai))

**My recommendation:** Use specific, actionable feedback, but don’t chase a score. Unless a checker provides credible validation, don’t interpret “85% ATS match” as an 85% chance of getting an interview.

Which checker are you using—and are you asking about its score or its suggested edits?

annotations.title: How to Read an Applicant Resume: Resume Review Tips
How to Use Screener Questions on Indeed
How to Read an Applicant Resume: Resume Review Tips
How to Read an Applicant Resume: Resume Review Tips
Resume Essentials Participant Guide 2026
How to Read an Applicant Resume: Resume Review Tips

content.text:
Assuming you mean **the first pass through your résumé**, the main question is: **“Is there enough relevant evidence here to justify a conversation?”** It’s an initial fit check, not a complete assessment of your potential. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&utm_source=openai))

Recruiters typically look for:

- **Must-have qualifications.** Required skills, experience, licenses or certifications—and practical requirements such as shift availability. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/resources/howtohub/how-to-use-screener-questions-on-indeed?utm_source=openai))
- **Relevant experience.** Have you done work similar to this role? Your job titles matter, but the responsibilities and skills underneath them help establish the actual match. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&utm_source=openai))
- **Appropriate experience level.** Does your background align with the role’s expected level of responsibility? ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&utm_source=openai))
- **Evidence of contribution.** Relevant accomplishments help show what you achieved, rather than merely what you were assigned to do. ([dol.gov](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/VETS/files/ResumeEssentials_PG_Interactive_Feb2026.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- **An easy-to-understand work history.** Clear roles, dates, skills and qualifications make it easier to assess your background. ([indeed.com](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/how-to-read-a-resume?co=US&utm_source=openai))

**My practical advice:** Make the top third of your résumé answer three questions without requiring inference:
1. What kind of work do you do?
2. Which key requirements do you meet?
3. What’s one concrete example of your impact?

For example, instead of “Results-oriented operations professional,” try something specific and truthful: “Operations analyst with four years in fulfillment; automated weekly reporting, saving six hours per week.”

Think **“make the match obvious,” not “include everything I’ve ever done.”**
